blocks.text: Roy DeCarava, Harlem Black and Blue
In Los Angeles, David Zwirner presents the fullest showing since 1983 of Roy DeCarava’s photographs of Black New York and its jazz, made from the late 1940s through the 1960s.
By Guénola Pellen. Photos by Roy DeCarava .

Roy DeCarava (1919–2009), a son of Harlem, became in 1952 the first African American photographer to win a Guggenheim Fellowship, championed by Edward Steichen, then head of photography at the Museum of Modern Art. For six decades he moved through the city with a handheld 35mm—light enough to carry him anywhere, intimate enough that he recognized himself in his subjects. “The process of making a photograph begins long before one even picks up the camera,” he said. Unlike most photographers of his day, he developed and printed every frame himself, coaxing from the darkroom a velvety black, almost painterly.

His pictures hold two inseparable worlds in one frame: the elegiac streets of Harlem—deliverymen on their rounds, children at play, riders waiting for the train—and the jazz greats. Miles Davis, John Coltrane, Elvin Jones, Ornette Coleman, Sarah Vaughan: DeCarava catches them mid-solo and offstage alike, insisting on their ordinary humanity as much as their genius. “Many of the best pictures show individuals—isolated, self-possessed, and, when performing, utterly absorbed in the act of creation,” observes Sherry Turner DeCarava, art historian and the photographer’s wife.

“I photograph musicians as people, not as musicians… What I respond to is their commitment to what they do. The intensity that they bring to life at that moment,” he said. To him, jazz and photography were kindred arts, two disciplines of the instant. He haunted the city’s clubs night after night, camera always in hand, in pursuit of what he called “images for the head and for the heart.”

In 1963 he photographed a demonstration by Black residents of a Brooklyn neighborhood whose homes were slated for demolition to expand the Downstate Medical Center; those who refused to move were carried away by the authorities. In Force, New York , he turns his lens on the bodies, the crowd, the dignity of the dispossessed—in whom he reads “the desire and the will by the majority of the people in the world to reach sunlight.” His work, Sherry Turner DeCarava adds, “found power in a visual course, more serene than turbulent.”

Across more than 130 silver gelatin prints, the exhibition draws us into his world: the bassist Edna Smith, eyes shut over her instrument; a couple folded into each other in the half-dark; the pensive face of the pianist Mary Lou Williams. “Each breath, each caress, each moment can only be seen by those who seek to see,” writes Ebony L. Haynes, a scholar of contemporary Black American aesthetics, who curated the show.
First shown in 1983 at the Studio Museum in Harlem, then just 125 prints, “the sound i saw” has not been seen at this scale since.
“Roy DeCarava: the sound i saw,” David Zwirner, Los Angeles, through October 31, 2026.
